mean: not knowing an unpleasant truth lets you stay at peace
lit: not knowing is being a Buddha: calm and untroubled, because you are unaware

use.how: Used as a predicate, often wryly about someone else who is unaware: 本人は知らぬが仏だ. Also a reason for not telling, or not wanting to hear, a painful truth.

cue: Your dad treasures a vase he thinks is a valuable antique. You know it is a cheap copy and decide it is kinder not to tell him.

mean: time is as valuable as money, so do not waste it

story.text: The Japanese saying translates the English proverb 'time is money', best known from Benjamin Franklin's letter of advice to a young tradesman. Franklin argued that a man who can earn ten shillings a day by his work, but idles away half the day, has not only spent what he paid for his amusement: he has also thrown away the five shillings he could have earned.
story.source: Benjamin Franklin, Advice to a Young Tradesman (1748)

use.how: Quoted whole as a reminder not to waste time, often about work or study: 時は金なりだから急ごう. The classical なり gives it a slightly stiff, motto-like ring.

near.diff: 光陰矢の如し remarks on how fast time flies; 時は金なり urges you to use time well because it has real value.

cue: Your boss cancels a long meeting that had no agenda, saying everyone's working hours are too valuable to throw away.
